title: Roman and Byzantine Palestine
subtitle: 135–638 AD · From Aelia Capitolina to the Muslim Conquest

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Aelia Capitolina, a Christian empire, and a Persian interruption

entries.label: Aelia Capitolina and a Purged Name
entries.hint: Following the Bar Kokhba Revolt's suppression, Hadrian rebuilt Jerusalem as the pagan colony Aelia Capitolina, barred Jews from entry, and renamed the province itself Syria Palaestina — a deliberate administrative erasure of the territory's Judean political identity that this folio's very own regional name still carries today, nearly nineteen centuries later.
entries.note: Compare herod-judea-63bc-135ce::c5 for the revolt and renaming itself, covered there as that folio's closing event.

entries.label: The Province Progressively Subdivided
entries.hint: Syria Palaestina was progressively split into smaller administrative units over the following centuries — Diocletian's reforms began the process, and by the early 5th century the territory had become Palaestina Prima (the coast and Judean hill country, governed from Caesarea), Palaestina Secunda (Galilee and the Golan) and Palaestina Tertia (the Negev and southern Transjordan) — a finer-grained provincial structure reflecting the territory's growing administrative and ecclesiastical importance to the empire.
entries.note: The exact staging of this subdivision across Diocletian's and subsequent reigns is not precisely dated in every particular by surviving sources, but the three-part Palaestina Prima/Secunda/Tertia structure is well attested by the early 5th century AD.

entries.label: Constantine's Conversion and Christian Patronage
entries.hint: Constantine's Edict of Milan granted legal toleration to Christianity across the empire, and his own patronage — funding major churches in Jerusalem and Bethlehem and elevating Christian clergy to unprecedented influence — began transforming Palestine from a province of largely incidental interest to a uniquely privileged holy land at the physical center of an increasingly Christian empire's religious imagination.
entries.note: Edict of Milan, 313 AD; Eusebius, Life of Constantine 3.25–43, on Constantine's Jerusalem church-building patronage.

entries.label: Julian's Pagan Restoration
entries.hint: The emperor Julian, attempting to reverse Constantine's Christianization and discredit Christian prophecy that the Jewish Temple would never be rebuilt, authorised and funded a Jewish effort to rebuild it in Jerusalem — construction was abruptly halted, according to the pagan contemporary historian Ammianus Marcellinus, by terrifying balls of fire bursting repeatedly from the foundations, a disruptive event Christian sources later took as providential intervention and modern historians more often attribute to an earthquake or underground gas ignition, with Julian's death in battle the following year ending the project permanently.
entries.note: Ammianus Marcellinus, Res Gestae 23.1.2–3, a non-Christian contemporary source independently attesting some disruptive physical event at the construction site.

entries.label: Justinian's Building and Legal Legacy
entries.hint: Justinian's reign brought the Byzantine Levant's building programme to its peak, including Jerusalem's enormous Nea Church, while his legal codification project (the Corpus Juris Civilis) formalised increasingly restrictive legal provisions against Jews and Samaritans that had been accumulating for generations — a reign combining monumental Christian architectural patronage with the empire's most systematic legal codification of religious minorities' diminished status.
entries.note: Procopius, On Buildings 5.6, on the Nea Church, dedicated 543 AD; the Codex Justinianus's provisions affecting Jews and Samaritans (Book 1, Title 5 and related titles).

entries.label: Persian Conquest and Byzantine Restoration
entries.hint: Sasanian Persian forces under Khosrow II captured Jerusalem in 614, carrying the relic of the True Cross into captivity at Ctesiphon — a Byzantine collapse only reversed a decade and a half later when Heraclius's counteroffensive forced a Persian withdrawal and the relic's negotiated return, restored to Jerusalem in a triumphant ceremony that proved, within less than a decade, to be Byzantine rule's final high point before permanent loss to a very different conqueror.
entries.note: Compare the Conflict entry on the 614 sack itself for the massacre and destruction; the True Cross's restoration is dated to 629 or 630 AD depending on the source.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Samaritan revolts, a Persian sack, and the Muslim conquest

entries.label: The Samaritan Revolts
entries.hint: The Samaritan community rose in armed revolt against Byzantine rule three times across seven decades, most seriously in 529 when Julian ben Sabar was crowned a rival king and the rebellion was crushed with such severity — mass killings, enslavement and forced conversion, by contemporary accounts, whose precise casualty figures are likely inflated but whose broad devastation is not seriously disputed — that the Samaritan population never recovered its earlier scale, reduced from a substantial regional community to the small remnant that survives to the present day.
entries.note: Procopius, Secret History 11.24–30; the 529 AD revolt is the best documented of the three, with the earlier 484 and later 556 AD uprisings attested more briefly.

entries.label: The Persian Sack of Jerusalem
entries.hint: Sasanian forces under the general Shahrbaraz stormed Jerusalem after a short siege, burned major churches including the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and killed a large number of the Christian population — a near-contemporary account attributed to the monk Strategios gives casualty figures in the tens of thousands that many modern historians treat as exaggerated in the manner typical of such accounts, while not doubting that a real and severe massacre took place.
entries.note: Strategios (Antiochus Strategos), The Capture of Jerusalem by the Persians in 614 AD, surviving in Georgian and Arabic translation.

entries.label: The Battle of Yarmouk
entries.hint: A decisive Rashidun Caliphate victory over a substantially larger Byzantine army along the Yarmouk River effectively ended organised Byzantine military resistance in Syria and Palestine, opening the way for the systematic Muslim conquest of the remaining Levantine cities over the following two years.
entries.note: al-Tabari, History of the Prophets and Kings, on the battle and its immediate aftermath; the Byzantine army's precise size is debated but its defeat's strategic decisiveness is not.

entries.label: Jerusalem's Surrender to Caliph Umar
entries.hint: Patriarch Sophronius negotiated Jerusalem's surrender personally with Caliph Umar, reportedly insisting the caliph himself come to receive the city's keys — the resulting agreement, later elaborated by tradition into the more detailed "Pact of Umar" whose precise wording scholars regard as a later formalisation rather than a verbatim 7th-century document, nonetheless established the basic pattern of protected but legally subordinate status for Christians and Jews that would structure the region's religious communities under Islamic rule for centuries afterward.
entries.note: al-Tabari and other early Islamic sources on Sophronius's surrender negotiations, 638 AD; the "Pact of Umar" text itself is generally dated by modern scholarship to a somewhat later period of elaboration rather than to 638 AD directly.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Provincial partition and an ecclesiastical hierarchy

entries.label: From Legion Garrison to Civil Province
entries.hint: Post-Bar-Kokhba Palestine was garrisoned by a full Roman legion stationed permanently at Legio (near Megiddo) rather than the smaller auxiliary forces earlier prefects had relied on — a substantially heavier military presence than before the revolt, reflecting Rome's judgement that the territory required standing legionary deterrence rather than light policing, even as day-to-day governance remained in civilian provincial hands based at Caesarea.
entries.note: The Legio VI Ferrata's permanent station at Legio (Caparcotna) near Megiddo from the mid-2nd century AD is archaeologically and epigraphically attested.

entries.label: Jerusalem's Elevation to a Patriarchate
entries.hint: The Council of Chalcedon elevated Jerusalem's bishopric to one of the church's five great patriarchates alongside Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria and Antioch, formal recognition of the city's unique religious significance overriding its comparatively modest administrative and demographic weight within the empire's ordinary civil hierarchy — an ecclesiastical status the city's practical political importance had never quite matched.
entries.note: Council of Chalcedon, 451 AD, Canon 28's broader hierarchy discussion and Jerusalem's confirmed patriarchal status.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Constantine's patronage, desert monks, a doctrinal split, and its limits

entries.label: Helena's Pilgrimage and Holy Site Identification
entries.hint: Constantine's mother Helena travelled to Palestine and, according to Eusebius, identified and marked the sites of Christ's birth and burial for church construction — the Church of the Nativity and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre that resulted became Christianity's two most important pilgrimage destinations, even though modern historians treat the precision of Helena's own site identifications, made three centuries after the events themselves, with the same caution as any late, tradition-driven attribution.
entries.note: Eusebius, Life of Constantine 3.25–43; Church of the Holy Sepulchre and Church of the Nativity, both begun under Constantine's patronage following Helena's visit.

entries.label: Legal Restrictions on a Shrinking Minority
entries.hint: Successive Christian emperors from Constantine onward progressively restricted Jewish and Samaritan legal rights — barring new synagogue construction in some periods, excluding Jews from imperial civil and military office, and eventually banning Jews from Jerusalem outright except on a single day of mourning each year — a steady legal tightening that accompanied, and reflected, the empire's broader transition from officially tolerating religious diversity to actively privileging Christian orthodoxy above it.
entries.note: Theodosian Code 16.8 and Codex Justinianus 1.5, the principal surviving legal collections documenting this progressive restriction across the 4th–6th centuries AD.

entries.label: Chalcedon and a Doctrinal Split
entries.hint: The Council of Chalcedon's ruling on Christ's nature was rejected by a substantial part of the Syrian and Egyptian church, whose adherents (later called Miaphysites, or pejoratively Monophysites, by their opponents) split into a separate church hierarchy — a division that fractured Christian unity across the eastern Levant for the rest of the Byzantine period and shaped the religious landscape the Ghassanid Arab Christian kingdom itself, further south, would inhabit as an adherent of the same rejected position.
entries.note: Council of Chalcedon, 451 AD; compare ghassanid-420-638 for the same Miaphysite Christian affiliation among the Ghassanid Arab federate kingdom to the Levant's south and east.

entries.label: Sabbas and the Judean Desert Monasteries
entries.hint: Sabbas the Sanctified founded a monastic community in a remote Judean desert gorge that grew into the Mar Saba monastery, part of a broader flourishing of desert asceticism across the Byzantine Levant that made Palestine, alongside Egypt, one of Christian monasticism's two most important formative regions — Mar Saba itself has remained continuously inhabited by monks from its founding to the present day, one of the longest unbroken religious communities anywhere in the world.
entries.note: Cyril of Scythopolis, Life of Sabas, the principal near-contemporary source for Sabbas's career and the Judean desert monastic movement generally.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: A mosaic map of the Holy Land, and monumental church architecture

entries.label: Byzantine Church Architecture at Its Height
entries.hint: Constantine's Church of the Holy Sepulchre and Church of the Nativity, followed two centuries later by Justinian's enormous Nea Church, represent successive high points of Byzantine ecclesiastical architecture specifically commissioned for the Holy Land's unique religious status — building projects whose scale and imperial funding had no real precedent in the region's earlier Roman-period architecture, itself typically civic or dynastic rather than devotional in purpose.
entries.note: Procopius, On Buildings 5.6, describing the Nea Church's scale and construction, completed 543 AD.
keywords: Constantine Church of the Holy Sepulchre

entries.label: The Madaba Map
entries.hint: A church floor at Madaba in modern Jordan preserves a vast mosaic map of the Byzantine Holy Land, its detailed depiction of Jerusalem — the walled city's colonnaded main street, gates and major churches all individually recognisable — making it the oldest surviving original cartographic representation of Jerusalem and one of the single most valuable artifacts for reconstructing the Byzantine-era city's actual physical layout.
entries.note: Madaba Map mosaic, Church of Saint George, Madaba, Jordan, conventionally dated to the second half of the 6th century AD.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Caesarea's biblical scholars and the first church historian

entries.label: Origen's Biblical Scholarship at Caesarea
entries.hint: The theologian Origen, forced from Alexandria after a dispute with his own bishop, relocated to Caesarea and built a renowned school and library there, producing the Hexapla — an immense six-column comparative edition setting the Hebrew Bible alongside multiple Greek translations — a work of textual scholarship so vast that only fragments survive today, but whose comparative method influenced biblical scholarship for centuries afterward.
entries.note: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 6.16, on Origen's Caesarea period and the Hexapla's composition.

entries.label: Eusebius, the First Church Historian
entries.hint: Eusebius, bishop of the same city of Caesarea where Origen had worked a generation earlier, wrote the Ecclesiastical History, the first sustained narrative history of Christianity from its origins to his own time, alongside an admiring biography of Constantine that, whatever its evident bias toward its imperial subject, remains a foundational primary source for virtually everything modern historians know about Constantine's specific religious policies in Palestine.
entries.note: Eusebius of Caesarea, Ecclesiastical History and Life of Constantine, both composed in the early-to-mid 4th century AD.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Gaza's wine amphorae crossing the Mediterranean

entries.label: Gaza Wine Crosses the Mediterranean
entries.hint: A distinctive amphora type manufactured around Gaza carried the region's wine across the Mediterranean in enormous quantities during Late Antiquity, with "Gaza jars" turning up in archaeological excavations as far away as Britain and the Black Sea — physical evidence of a genuinely long-distance export trade that made Palestine's Byzantine-era coastal economy considerably more prosperous and internationally connected than its earlier Roman-period footprint.
entries.note: "Gaza amphorae" (Late Roman Amphora 4), a well-documented and widely distributed Late Antique ceramic type identified at find-sites across the Mediterranean and beyond.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Desert runoff farming feeds a Byzantine boom

entries.label: Negev Runoff Farming Feeds a Boom
entries.hint: Byzantine-era farmers in the arid Negev built elaborate systems of channels, terraces and check-dams to capture and concentrate the desert's scarce, unpredictable rainfall runoff onto small cultivated plots, sustaining substantial towns like Avdat and Shivta in territory that supports only sparse vegetation without this deliberate hydraulic intervention — an agricultural technology that let the Byzantine Levant's population and prosperity extend well beyond the better-watered coastal and highland zones.
entries.note: Archaeological survey and reconstruction of Byzantine-era Negev runoff agriculture systems at Avdat, Shivta, Halutza and related sites, 4th–7th centuries AD.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: A pilgrimage economy connects the Christian world

entries.label: A Pilgrimage Economy Connects the Christian World
entries.hint: An anonymous traveller from Bordeaux left the earliest surviving detailed Christian pilgrim itinerary in 333 AD, the first of a steadily growing stream of pilgrims from across the Christian world whose travel, lodging and devotional purchases created a substantial and enduring pilgrimage economy — hostels, guides, relic trade and church income — that connected Palestine's local economy directly to patterns of piety and travel originating as far away as Gaul and Spain.
entries.note: Itinerarium Burdigalense ("Bordeaux Itinerary"), 333 AD, the earliest surviving Christian pilgrim travel account; compare the Lives entry on Egeria's later, more personally detailed pilgrimage account.
keywords: Pilgrimage Economy Connects the Christian World

entries.label: Byzantium's Contested Eastern Frontier
entries.hint: Palestine's five centuries under Roman and then Byzantine rule ran alongside a much longer contest for control of the broader Near East against Parthia and then Sasanian Persia, a rivalry that occasionally spilled directly into the Levant itself, as in 614, and that had already exhausted both empires financially and militarily by the time a third, entirely unanticipated power emerged from Arabia in the 630s to displace them both from the region within a single decade.
entries.note: Comparative framing of the centuries-long Roman/Byzantine-Parthian/Sasanian rivalry and its role in weakening both empires ahead of the 7th-century Arab conquests.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: A nun's travel diary, and an eyewitness to a massacre

entries.label: Egeria's Pilgrimage Diary
entries.hint: A woman named Egeria, probably a nun travelling from Gaul or Spain, wrote a long, vivid letter-diary for the religious community back home describing her journey through the Holy Land in remarkable personal detail — the liturgy she witnessed in Jerusalem, the terrain she crossed, the local clergy who guided her — making it one of the earliest substantial surviving works by a named woman author and an unusually direct, unmediated personal voice from the whole Late Antique period.
entries.note: Itinerarium Egeriae (Egeria's Travels), the surviving manuscript fragment covering roughly 381–384 AD; her precise origin (Gaul versus Spain) remains debated among scholars.

entries.label: A Monk's Account of the 614 Massacre
entries.hint: The monk Strategios's account of the Persian sack describes, in harrowing personal-witness style, bodies filling the streets and cisterns of Jerusalem and the desperate efforts of survivors to bury the dead in mass graves — a text whose specific casualty numbers modern historians treat cautiously as likely inflated, but whose underlying testimony to a community's direct experience of sudden, catastrophic violence remains a rare and valuable survival from the period.
entries.note: Strategios (Antiochus Strategos), The Capture of Jerusalem by the Persians in 614 AD.
